name: The Grant household — a documented attorney, unplaced in the town
head: grant_james

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE PAPER, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The corpus first prints this person at the Democrat of 3 September 1834, column 10, so they are in the town's paper by 1834-09-03 and at no stated time before it; nothing reached says when they came. Last printed 1835-06-10.

arrival_year.note: THE MAN'S OWN RECOLLECTION, NOT A CONTEMPORARY RECORD. He registered at the Calumet Club on the roll of 1879 and gave 1834, April 23, as his date of coming to Chicago — forty-four years after the fact. The roll's own `arrival_year_basis` says it dates the claim and does not prove it, so the year is carried at `inferred` and the household's `arrival` block keeps the bound the contemporary evidence sets.

origin.note: A BIRTHPLACE, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME CLAIM. The Calumet Club roll of 1879 gives “Enfield, North Carolina.” as where this man was BORN; this field asks where the household came FROM, and a generation that moved west in stages frequently did not come from the state it was born in. It is carried as the best statement of origin the sources make about this household and not as a last residence.

reason_for_coming.value: A professional practice in a new county seat
reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THIS HOUSEHOLD'S OWN RECORDED TRADE, WHICH IS NOT ITS MOTIVE. The head is recorded as attorney, and this names the documented draw that trade answered in this town in this decade. It does not claim to know why these people came. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

basis.note: arrival_fill.trade_reasons.a_practice_in_a_new_county_seat — the head's recorded trade is evidence about this household, and the draw it answered is the reason the record will carry until a source states one.

replaceable_by.match: a source that says why this household came, or a committed source that apportions the town's arrivals between the land sales, the canal and the harbour works

lives_at.note: Not attested. NOTHING IS BEING WITHHELD HERE: no source reached says where this person lived, and 52 households in this dataset were already in that position before this one was written.

works_at.note: Not attested as a structure this project models. The trade is documented; the premises are not one of the committed records.

last_dated_appearance.note: NO SIGHTING, SO THE LEG IS A SOURCE'S SPAN. The card holds no dated reading of this person at or before the scene date; the date here is the far end of what a cited source COVERS, which the role's own note calls the source's bound and not the man's. Read from `roles[] (source_span)` as `1833-11/1835-08`, which reaches 1835-08-31 — a window that covers 1835-07-01 itself, so it pins no last sighting before the day and cannot be read as one. THE FIELD IS THE EVIDENCE UNDER THE VERDICT, not a new claim: nothing here moves the presence off `uncertain`, and T-1159 and T-1172 classify this household by this date instead of reading it out of the prose (T-1144 acceptance 9).

present_on_scene_date.note: THE CORPUS STOPS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Last printed 1835-06-10, at the Democrat of 10 June 1835, column 8, and nothing reached either follows this person to 1 July 1835 or says they left. A documented resident whose whereabouts on one day are unknown is `uncertain` here rather than dropped: that is the same distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and it is a finding rather than a gap.

persons.name: James Grant

occupation.note: THE TRADE IS THE PAPER'S. The corpus reads it as regimental adjutant, attorney, counsellor at law, at the Democrat of 3 September 1834, column 10; the Democrat of 10 June 1835, column 8. The residents vocabulary's nearest period-correct word for it is `attorney`, and where the corpus prints more than one trade they are all named here rather than reduced to the one the vocabulary could take.

Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source EARLIER than the scene date corroborates and dates and never promotes: a man on a roll of 1833, 1834 or 1835 is not thereby at Chicago on 1 July 1835. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT. The reading of the roll is documented — the town's own paper, held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository, twice mediated by Schulz's transcription and Genealogy Trails' republication, which this project has not gone behind. What no source states is that the man on the roll is the person on this card: data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json joins them on a name, by its rule “one resident of the surname 'Grant' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered.”, and forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'J. Grant' against resident 'James Grant'. A bound whose subject is inferred is an inferred bound. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source EARLIER than the scene date corroborates and dates and never promotes, and a source LATER than it does not promote either. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT: the issue is deposited, dated and numbered in data/research/newspapers/corpus.json, and what no source states is that the name the paper prints is the person on this card — the register joins them under its own written note. persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'J. GRANT, Jr.' and 'JAMES GRANT' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 3 September 1834, column 10; the Democrat of 10 June 1835, column 8. The corpus associates the name with Chicago, La Salle Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `attorney` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Grant, J.” (poll_1835_026, line 313). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Grant' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Grant, James, | 1834, April 23, | Enfield, North Carolina. | 66 | Davenport, Iowa.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “J. Grant” (f1839_v0641, printed page 45, ward 6, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Grant' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins J. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Grant, John C. | Letter. | December 29, 1875.” (second_presb_0171, printed page 163), admitted 1875-12-29 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Grant' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 11 times, as “GRANT JAMES”, 1836-06-28: 11 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 6 in the town the register codes CHI (L1BL6CHI, as printed); lot 10 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHI (L10B2CHI, as printed); lot 10 of block 5 in the town the register codes CHI (L10BL5CHI, as printed); lot 2 of block 4 in the town the register codes CHI (L2BL4CHI, as printed); lot 2 of block 6 in the town the register codes CHI (L2BL6CHI, as printed); lot 4 of block 6 in the town the register codes CHIV (L4BL6CHIV, as printed); lot 5 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHI (L5BL2CHI, as printed); lot 6 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHI (L6BL2CHI, as printed); lot 7 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHI (L7BL2CHI, as printed); lot 8 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHI (L8BL2CHI, as printed); lot 9 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHI (L9BL2CHI, as printed), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $28120.00 (ls1185, ls1186, ls1187, ls1188, ls1189, ls1190, ls1191, ls1192, ls1193, ls1194, ls1195). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $28120.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: GRANT JAMES matches James Grant: the forename names James Grant of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

resident_research.summary: Matched on the 1835 poll list as 'Grant, J.', and the identification is held by trade across three decades: Fergus 1839 prints 'Grant, Jas., attorney, N. Water st near Rush, bds. Lake House' and the old-settler notice 'Grant, James, lawyer, died, Oakland, Cal., Mar. 14, 1891, aged 78'. The 1891 age puts his birth at 1812-13, which makes him about 22 in the scene.

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

age_band.note: THE BAND THIS PERSON'S OWN BIRTH YEAR PUTS THEM IN on 1 July 1835. It is a view of a value already on this card and adds nothing to it; it exists so the age axis can be read across the whole layer at once, beside the bands the model draws for everybody else.

sex_basis.note: A FORENAME THAT STANDS IN ONE SEX'S NAMING ONLY. 'James' is read as male because 2 persons in this layer whose sex a source records bear it (couch_james, kinzie_james), and it stands in the irish and yankee male forename pool of this town's own attested naming. Nothing about this person is recorded; the name is the whole of the reasoning, and the table that licenses it — data/research/residents/forename_sex.json — refuses a name its own evidence splits, refuses Jean, Marion, Leslie and Francis by name, and refuses an initial outright.

birth_year.note: A BIRTH INTERVAL OUT OF A MAN'S OWN STATEMENT OF HIS AGE. He registered at the Calumet Club's reception to the settlers of Chicago on 27 May 1879 and gave his age as 66: "Grant, James, | 1834, April 23, | Enfield, North Carolina. | 66 | Davenport, Iowa.". An age of 66 completed years given on that day means the birth falls after 27 May 1812 and on or before 27 May 1813, so the birth year is 1812 or 1813. The subtraction is this project's; the page states no year of birth. IT IS A RECOLLECTION, forty-four years after the scene date — better than a recollection about somebody else, and still not a record. The merge onto this person is the old-settler crosswalk's own (OS1), in data/research/old_settlers/people.json.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name James Grant as a attorney at Chicago 2 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

old_settler_deaths.the_header_admission:
Names, places * , dates, and ages at death
of some of Chicago's Old Settlers, prior to 1843, and other well - known citizens who arrived after 1843, together
with others prominently connected with Illinois history:
old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. grant_james, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e0576 (a single entry).
